hypotheses.title: SignatureVerifier v-check always reverts (v != 27 || v != 28)
hypotheses.description: The condition `if (v != 27 || v != 28) revert InvalidSignature();` is always true because v cannot simultaneously equal both 27 and 28. Every signature verification reverts, permanently breaking any flow that relies on this library (e.g., RNG callback validation if used). The intended check is `v != 27 && v != 28`.
hypotheses.attackPath: Any external actor calling a function that routes through `SignatureVerifier.recover` will always revert; if the library is used to gate a privileged action, the action becomes permanently uncallable (DoS). Conversely, if the check were meant to reject invalid v, it fails to do so.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent denial of service for any signature-gated functionality; if used for authorization, could also allow bypass depending on caller handling.
hypotheses.recommendation: Replace with `if (v != 27 && v != 28) revert InvalidSignature();`.

hypotheses.title: RewardsManager claims WETH yield but passes USDB address
hypotheses.description: When claiming WETH yield, the code calls `IERC20YieldClaimable(_contract).claimERC20Yield(address(USDB), _yieldWETH)` — passing the USDB address instead of WETH. The `_yieldWETH` amount is then forwarded to the distributor as WETH, but the underlying claim was executed against USDB, so the WETH yield is never actually claimed while USDB is claimed twice (once for USDB, once for WETH). This corrupts yield accounting and can drain USDB yield to the wrong token bag.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Any caller invokes `claimYieldForContracts([victimContract])`. 2. `_claimYieldForContract` claims USDB yield correctly, then calls `claimERC20Yield(USDB, _yieldWETH)` — claiming additional USDB yield equal to the WETH claimable amount. 3. The returned `_yieldWETH` is forwarded to the distributor as WETH, but no WETH was actually claimed, so the distributor's WETH transferFrom fails or the accounting is wrong. 4. USDB yield is over-claimed and misattributed.
hypotheses.impact: Yield misattribution, potential revert of yield distribution, loss of USDB yield accounting integrity.
hypotheses.recommendation: Change the WETH branch to `claimERC20Yield(address(WETH), _yieldWETH)`.

hypotheses.title: Silently typo claims WETH yield as USDB, funds sent to wrong token
hypotheses.description: When handling WETH, the code calls `IERC20YieldClaimable(_contract).claimERC20Yield(address(USDB), _yieldWETH)` — passing `USDB` instead of `WETH` as the token contract. Any claim for WETH yield will therefore attempt to claim USDB for the contract's WETH-rebasing balance; either reverting (DoS), or worse, if the child contract has a matching USDB balance, USDB is drained while `_yieldWETH` accounting still increments, mismatching `tokenBags` and double-counting.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Any untrusted caller triggers `claimYieldForContracts([someContract])` on a contract that has both WETH rebasing accrual and USDB balance. 2. The WETH branch invokes `claimERC20Yield(USDB, _yieldWETH)`, moving USDB out of the child contract to the RewardsManager. 3. `_yieldWETH` still forwarded to distributor as WETH bag, but actual WETH was never pulled → later USDB.approve for distributor may over-distribute or revert.
hypotheses.impact: Misappropriation of USDB yield; accounting mismatch between claimed shares and forwarded token bags; potential theft of another contract's USDB rebasing rewards.
hypotheses.recommendation: Pass `address(WETH)` in the WETH branch: `IERC20YieldClaimable(_contract).claimERC20Yield(address(WETH), _yieldWETH);`.

hypotheses.title: MigrationManager.migrateAllNFTs lets arbitrary caller migrate another user's NFTs
hypotheses.description: `migrateAllNFTs(address _user, uint32 _skip)` has no caller check. Its sibling `burnNFTs` and `burnRemainingPurchasedNFTs` explicitly check `_user != msg.sender` and require the user to have chosen a matching `UserLockedChoice`. Here there is no `msg.sender == _user` requirement and no role restriction. Any untrusted address can call `migrateAllNFTs(victim, 0)` and cause the contract to iterate `_userTokenIds[victim]`, mark snapshots claimed, mint new NFTs to `_user` via `_nftOverlord.mintForMigration`, burn old NFTs, and — critically — invoke `_lockManager.lockOnBehalf{value: quantity}(...)` with the caller's ETH to fund the victim's lock.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Victim calls `lockFundsForAllMigration()` which sets `_userLockedAction[victim] = LOCKED_FULL_MIGRATION` and holds their tokens in MigrationManager. 2) Attacker (any address) calls `migrateAllNFTs(victim, 0)`. 3) The function authenticates only `_userLockedAction[_user] == LOCKED_FULL_MIGRATION`, never `msg.sender == _user`. It then processes the migration with `msg.value` supplied by the attacker.
hypotheses.impact: An attacker can force migration paths and consume the full migration quota for a victim, minting replacement NFTs to them before they choose; if the attacker supplies ETH for a USDB/WETH migration, the caller's value is consumed, and the victim's lockable balances and snapshot state are irreversibly claimed.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `if (_user != msg.sender) revert UnauthorizedError();` or require a role/admin path when migrating on behalf of another user.

hypotheses.title: BonusManager._calculateMigrationBonus divides by (migrateHighestAmount - weightedValue)
hypotheses.description: When `weightedValue` is between `halfAmount` and `migrateHighestAmount`, the bonus is computed as `(migrationBonus * (weightedValue - halfAmount)) / (migrateHighestAmount - weightedValue)`. As `weightedValue` approaches `migrateHighestAmount`, the denominator approaches zero, causing the bonus to explode (or revert on overflow). The intended linear interpolation should divide by `(migrateHighestAmount - halfAmount)`, not by `(migrateHighestAmount - weightedValue)`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker migrates a large amount to set `migrateHighestAmount` high. 2) Attacker locks tokens so `weightedValue` is just below `migrateHighestAmount`. 3) `getHarvestBonus` returns a near-infinite bonus, which is applied in `AccountManager._harvest` to multiply daily schnibbles. 4) Attacker harvests enormous schnibbles and converts them to points/tokens.
hypotheses.impact: Unbounded harvest bonus → attacker mints arbitrary schnibbles, drains ClaimManager points, and mints MunchToken via `convertPointsToTokens`.
hypotheses.recommendation: Change the denominator to `(migrateHighestAmount - halfAmount)` and clamp the result to `migrationBonus`.

hypotheses.title: RewardsManager.claimGasFeeForContracts callable by anyone drains gas yield
hypotheses.description: Unlike the commented-out `claimGasFee()` which is guarded by `onlyRole(Role.ClaimYield)`, the live `claimGasFeeForContracts(address[] calldata _contracts)` has no access modifier. Any untrusted external caller can invoke it for arbitrary `_contracts` addresses, forcing the contract to call `blastContract.claimMaxGas(_contracts[i], address(this))` and forward the received ETH to `gasFeeDistributor`. The only requirement is that `_contracts[i]` has authorized this contract as a gas claimer on Blast, so the attacker can drain all accurable gas yield at will.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker monitors configured gas-collector contracts authorized to RewardsManager. 2) Attacker calls `claimGasFeeForContracts([contractA, contractB, ...])` directly. 3) For each address, `blastContract.claimMaxGas` sweeps accrued gas ETH into RewardsManager and it is immediately forwarded to `gasFeeDistributor.receiveTokens{value: _gas}`. 4) Attacker can repeat at any time to front-run or steal the intended distribution, denying the protocol any control over when/how gas fees are claimed.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of protocol-controlled yield timing and funds; any third party can trigger gas claims at will and force distribution to the configured distributor, locking the protocol out of its own privileged yield-collection workflow.
hypotheses.recommendation: Wrap `claimGasFeeForContracts` (and the analogous yield variant) with `onlyRole(Role.ClaimYield)` matching the original commented-out implementation.

hypotheses.title: SnuggeryManager.pet multiplies schnibbles by 1e18 after division
hypotheses.description: `PET_TOTAL_SCHNIBBLES` is configured as `10e18 / 72` (per comment). The code computes `petterSchnibbles = ((totalSchnibbles * 5) / 11) * 1e18` and `pettedSchnibbles = ((totalSchnibbles * 6) / 11) * 1e18`. The `* 1e18` is applied AFTER the division, inflating the credited schnibbles by 1e18 relative to the intended unit. Since `totalSchnibbles` is already in 1e18-scale units, multiplying by 1e18 again produces astronomically large unfedSchnibbles balances.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker registers two accounts (petter and petted) with a snuggery NFT. 2) Calls `pet` from the petter account on the petted account's NFT. 3) Both accounts receive schnibbles inflated by 1e18. 4) Attacker feeds these schnibbles to their NFTs to gain massive chonks, level up, and dominate ClaimManager point distribution.
hypotheses.impact: Unbounded schnibble inflation → attacker captures nearly all claimable points each period, draining the emission pool and breaking the game economy.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove the trailing `* 1e18` (or divide by 1e18 if the intent was to scale down), and unit-test the resulting magnitudes against `PET_TOTAL_SCHNIBBLES`.

hypotheses.title: SignatureVerifier accepts malleable signatures and wrong v check
hypotheses.description: The check `if (v != 27 || v != 28) revert InvalidSignature();` is always true (a value cannot be both 27 and 28), so any signature with v == 27 or v == 28 reverts, and signatures with other v values also revert. This makes the library unusable for valid signatures and, more importantly, the logic is inverted from the intended check. Additionally, there is no check for s-value malleability (s > secp256k1n/2), allowing signature malleability if the check were fixed.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A legitimate signer produces a valid signature with v = 27 or 28. 2) Any contract using SignatureVerifier.recover() reverts, blocking the intended flow. 3) If the check is later fixed to `v != 27 && v != 28`, an attacker can still submit a malleated signature (s' = n - s) that recovers the same address, potentially bypassing replay protections that rely on signature uniqueness.
hypotheses.impact: DoS of signature-based flows; potential replay/malleability issues if the check is corrected without adding s-value bounds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `if (v != 27 && v != 28) revert InvalidSignature();` and enforce s <= secp256k1n/2 to prevent malleability.

hypotheses.title: MigrationManager lockFundsForAllMigration ignores ERC20 transfer return
hypotheses.category: Unchecked return value on external token
hypotheses.description: `IERC20(tokenContract).transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), totalLockAmount)` is called without checking the boolean return value. Non-reverting ERC20s (e.g., USDT-style or tokens returning false) will silently fail, yet `_userLockedAction[msg.sender]` is set to `LOCKED_FULL_MIGRATION` and the event is emitted. The user is then considered migrated without funds actually being transferred.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker uses a token that returns false on transferFrom (or a token whose transferFrom silently fails). 2. Calls `lockFundsForAllMigration` with `msg.value == 0`. 3. Contract records the migration as locked without receiving tokens. 4. Attacker later calls `migrateAllNFTs` to mint new NFTs backed by nothing.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker mints migration NFTs without paying; protocol loses the locked funds backing those NFTs.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `SafeERC20.safeTransferFrom` or require the returned bool is true.

hypotheses.title: LockManager._lock ignores ERC20 transferFrom return value
hypotheses.category: Unchecked return value on external token
hypotheses.description: `token.transferFrom(_tokenOwner, address(this), _quantity)` is called without checking the return value. For non-reverting ERC20s that return false, the lock is recorded (`lockedToken.quantity += _quantity`) and NFTs are queued via `nftOverlord.addReveal`, but no tokens are actually received. The user can later `unlock` and drain real tokens deposited by other users.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker configures a token that returns false on transferFrom (or uses a token with such behavior). 2. Calls `lock(token, quantity)` — allowance check passes, transferFrom returns false silently. 3. `lockedToken.quantity` is incremented and reveal NFTs are queued. 4. Attacker calls `unlock` after lock duration to withdraw real tokens from the contract's pooled balance.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of pooled locked tokens; protocol insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `SafeERC20.safeTransferFrom` or require the returned bool is true.

hypotheses.title: getLockedWeightedValue underflows for tokens with decimals > 18
hypotheses.description: The function computes deltaDecimal = 10 ** (18 - configuredTokens[token].decimals). If an admin configures a token whose decimals value is greater than 18 (e.g., a token with 24 decimals), the subtraction underflows and the call reverts. Because this function is called by AccountManager.getDailySchnibbles() and BonusManager.getHarvestBonus(), any player with such a token locked cannot harvest or claim points.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Admin configures a token with decimals > 18 (or a malicious token is added via configureToken). 2) A player locks that token. 3) Any call to harvest(), claimPoints(), or getHarvestBonus() for that player reverts due to the underflow in getLockedWeightedValue().
hypotheses.impact: Frozen funds / DoS: affected players cannot harvest, claim points, or receive bonuses until the token is removed or the code is upgraded.
hypotheses.recommendation: Reject tokens with decimals > 18 in configureToken, or compute the scaling factor using a safe branch (e.g., divide instead of multiply when decimals > 18).

hypotheses.title: RNGProxy request index collision allows overwriting pending requests
hypotheses.description: `requests[_index]` is keyed only by a caller-supplied `_index`. NFTOverlord uses `revealIndex = uint160(mainAccount) | (revealNonce << 160)` for reveals, but `mintFromPrimordial` and `munchableFed` (levelUp) use `uint256(uint160(_player))` and `_tokenId` respectively with no nonce. If a player has both a pending reveal and a pending primordial/levelUp request, or two levelUp requests for the same token, the second `requestRandom` overwrites the first RequestData. When the first callback arrives, it executes the second request's selector/target with the first request's index, and the second callback then reverts with NoRequestError.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted player triggers `startReveal()` (index = address|nonce<<160) and then `mintFromPrimordial` (index = address) — different keys, but a player can also trigger two `munchableFed` level-ups on the same token before the first RNG callback lands (e.g. by feeding twice via SnuggeryManager), causing the second `requestRandom` to overwrite the first. The first callback then executes the second request's data, and the second callback reverts.
hypotheses.impact: RNG callbacks misroute to the wrong selector/target, causing stuck reveals/level-ups, incorrect NFT attribute assignment, and permanent loss of the RNG response (funds spent on RNG wasted; user NFTs stuck in unrevealed/level-up limbo).
hypotheses.recommendation: Include a monotonically increasing per-contract nonce in the request key (as done for reveals) for all request types, or reject a new request if `requests[_index].targetContract != address(0)`.

hypotheses.title: ClaimManager._claimPoints referral bonus not deducted from claimAmount
hypotheses.description: `_claimPoints` computes `claimAmount` from the player's share of `availablePoints`, then adds `_referralBonus = (claimAmount * bonusManager.getReferralBonus()) / 1e18` to the referrer's `_points` WITHOUT subtracting it from `claimAmount` or from `currentPeriod.available`. The comment even notes "Think about ways to keep this within total emission instead of adding to the total count". This means total points minted per period can exceed `pointsPerPeriod`, and the excess is silently added to the system.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker registers many accounts with themselves as referrer. 2) Each account harvests and claims points, generating referral bonuses for the attacker's main account. 3) The attacker accumulates points beyond the per-period emission cap. 4) Attacker converts excess points to MunchToken via `convertPointsToTokens`, inflating token supply beyond intended emission.
hypotheses.impact: Inflation of MunchToken supply and points beyond the configured `pointsPerPeriod`, diluting other players and breaking tokenomics.
hypotheses.recommendation: Deduct `_referralBonus` from `claimAmount` (or from `currentPeriod.available`) so total emission per period is bounded.

hypotheses.title: Migration bonus uses stale usdPrice and can divide by zero
hypotheses.description: The migration bonus is computed from configuredToken.usdPrice, which is only updated via the multisig price feed and can be zero or stale. If usdPrice is 0, migrateHighestAmount and halfAmount become 0, and the branch weightedValue >= migrateHighestAmount is taken, granting the full migrationBonus regardless of actual locked value. Additionally, the formula (migrationBonus * (weightedValue - halfAmount)) / (migrateHighestAmount - weightedValue) can divide by zero when weightedValue equals migrateHighestAmount in the else-if branch.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker waits until usdPrice for the migrated token is 0 (e.g., before the first price update or after a malicious update). 2) Attacker migrates a small amount. 3) getHarvestBonus() returns the full migrationBonus because weightedValue >= 0. 4) Alternatively, attacker arranges weightedValue == migrateHighestAmount to trigger division by zero and revert harvests.
hypotheses.impact: Inflated harvest bonuses (reward inflation) or DoS of harvest for affected players.
hypotheses.recommendation: Guard against usdPrice == 0 and migrateHighestAmount == weightedValue before computing the bonus; use a safe fallback when the price is unset.

hypotheses.title: LockManager.lockOnBehalf allows locking on behalf of any registered account without consent
hypotheses.description: `lockOnBehalf` accepts an arbitrary `_onBehalfOf` and locks tokens into that account's `lockedTokens` mapping. The function only checks that `_onBehalfOf` is a registered main account (`_mainAccount == _lockRecipient`), but does not require any authorization from `_onBehalfOf`. An attacker can lock 1 wei of a configured token (or ETH) on behalf of any victim, which calls `accountManager.forceHarvest(_lockRecipient)` and `nftOverlord.addReveal(_lockRecipient, ...)`, and overwrites `lockedToken.unlockTime` and `playerSettings[_lockRecipient].lockDuration`. This can extend the victim's unlock time and reset their lock duration, and can also inflate their `unrevealedNFTs` count.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker calls `lockOnBehalf(token, 1, victim)` with a tiny amount. The victim's `lockedToken.unlockTime` is reset to `block.timestamp + _lockDuration`, potentially extending a previously shorter lock, and `playerSettings[victim].lockDuration` is overwritten. The victim's `unrevealedNFTs` is incremented, and `forceHarvest` is triggered (which is benign but state-changing).
hypotheses.impact: Griefing: victim's lock duration and unlock time can be manipulated, delaying their ability to unlock; victim's `unrevealedNFTs` count is inflated, potentially causing them to receive unexpected NFTs or hit `MAX_REVEAL_QUEUE`. No direct fund loss but denial of unlock and state corruption.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `msg.sender == _onBehalfOf` or an explicit approval/allowance from `_onBehalfOf` before allowing `lockOnBehalf`.

hypotheses.title: USD price update can be executed with stale/zero price and no sanity bounds
hypotheses.description: The USD price for configured tokens is set purely by a 3-of-5 multisig of PriceFeed roles via proposeUSDPrice/approveUSDPrice, with no bounds, no deviation check, and no freshness requirement. A single proposer can propose an arbitrary price (including 0 or an absurdly large value) and only two additional approvals are needed to commit it. Because getLockedWeightedValue() and BonusManager._calculateMigrationBonus() consume configuredTokens[].usdPrice directly, a wrong price immediately distorts locked value, harvest rewards, and migration bonuses.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker compromises or colludes with 3 PriceFeed role keys (or a single proposer plus two approvers). 2) proposeUSDPrice(0, [token]) is submitted. 3) Two other PriceFeed accounts call approveUSDPrice(0). 4) _execUSDPriceUpdate writes usdPrice = 0 for the token. 5) All players' getLockedWeightedValue() returns 0, harvest yields drop to zero, and migration bonus math divides by zero or returns zero.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong accounting of locked value and rewards; harvest and migration bonuses can be zeroed or inflated arbitrarily, causing loss of user rewards and potential division-by-zero reverts in BonusManager.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce a non-zero price, a maximum deviation from the previous price, and a maximum staleness window before applying the update; also require the proposal to be executed within a bounded time.

hypotheses.title: LockManager.unlock reverts on zero-value ETH transfer to contract recipient
hypotheses.description: When `_tokenContract == address(0)`, `unlock` uses `payable(msg.sender).transfer(_quantity)`. If `msg.sender` is a contract that reverts on receiving ETH (e.g., a smart-contract wallet with a reverting `receive`, or a contract with no payable fallback), the transfer reverts and the entire unlock call reverts. The user's locked ETH remains stuck because there is no alternative withdrawal path.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a contract wallet that reverts on ETH receipt. 2) Attacker locks ETH via `lock(address(0), qty)` from that contract. 3) After unlockTime, attacker calls `unlock(address(0), qty)` — the `transfer` reverts, so the ETH is permanently locked. (Also affects any user whose wallet later becomes non-payable, e.g., via upgrade.)
hypotheses.impact: Locked ETH becomes permanently unrecoverable for affected users; no recovery function exists.
hypotheses.recommendation: Replace `transfer` with a pull-pattern withdrawal (credit a `pendingWithdrawals` mapping and let users call `withdraw()`), or use `call{value:...}("")` and handle failure without reverting the state update.

hypotheses.title: claimPoints can be re-triggered each period with same chonk, referral double-dip
hypotheses.description: `_claimPoints` mints points to `_points[_player]` based on `getTotalChonk(_player) / currentPeriod.globalTotalChonk * availablePoints`, and also awards a referral bonus to `player.referrer` each period. The global chonk snapshot is only updated on `newPeriod()` via `snuggeryManager.getGlobalTotalChonk()`, but individual chonk can change (feed, import, export) after the snapshot. Because `getTotalChonk` reads live attributes while the denominator is stale, a player can inflate their ratio relative to the snapshot, or more directly, the same chonk is rewarded every period without any offsetting cost. A referrer accumulates points every period for each referred player's claim, effectively perpetual free points.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker registers account A with referrer B (or self-controlled B). 2. Farm chonk cheaply in period N. 3. Every new period, call `claimPoints()` — points are minted based on the (now stale) global denominator; if any other players reduce chonk, attacker's share grows. 4. Referrer B also earns points repeatedly per period for the same chonk, with no cap or one-time limit. 5. Convert accumulated points via `convertPointsToTokens`.
hypotheses.impact: Unlimited point inflation → MunchToken minted against phantom emissions; dilution of honest participants; protocol token insolvency if `pointsPerPeriod` is finite.
hypotheses.recommendation: Snapshot per-player chonk at period start or use a checkpointed share; make referral bonus one-time or capped per period and bounded by the referred player's actual claimed amount.

hypotheses.title: BaseRNGProxy.requestRandom selector stored unverified enables arbitrary callback target
hypotheses.description: `requestRandom(address _contract, bytes4 _selector, uint256 _index)` stores any `(targetContract, selector)` pair keyed by an attacker-chosen `_index`. It is guarded by `onlyConfiguredContract(StorageKey.NFTOverlord)`, so only NFTOverlord can call it. However NFTOverlord itself uses `rngProxy.requestRandom(address(this), keccak256("reveal(uint256,bytes)"), revealIndex)` where `revealIndex = uint256(uint160(_mainAccount)) | (revealNonce[_mainAccount] << 160)`. In `_callback`, the stored data is used to perform `data.targetContract.call(callData)` — the callee is whatever was stored, and the selector any bytes4 the caller supplied. Since NFTOverlord is a trusted configured contract, this alone is not attacker-reachable. The exposure is in the derived classes: `RNGProxySelfHosted.provideRandom` (role-gated) and `RNGProxyAPI3.provideRandom` (Airnode-gated) both forward the same `_callback`. Because `_index` is fully attacker-influenceable via NFTOverlord’s revealIndex derivation from `_mainAccount`, a sub-account that reveals NFT will write a request keyed by the main account’s address-as-uint256, potentially colliding with future reveal slots.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Player A (`0xaaa...`) triggers reveal, writing request at index `uint160(0xaaa...) | (0 << 160)`. 2) Player B has an address such that `uint160(playerB) | (nonce << 160)` equals an index already used by another account (e.g., if two addresses differ only by high bits, or via revealNonce increments in the low range). 3) When the oracle delivers randomness, `_callback` reads the pre-existing RequestData and re-invokes the wrong target with attacker-controlled selector.
hypotheses.impact: Callback confusion can direct randomness to the wrong target contract, causing reveal misrouting, level-up corruption, or state corruption in the target when the target accepts arbitrary calls. The stored `bytes4` selector is not constrained by anything the RNG contracts can validate.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce at `requestRandom` that `_contract == address(this)` (or reserve target contract from config) and restrict the allowed selectors to the contract’s own reveal/level-up functions, or use per-caller request counters instead of address-derived indexes.

hypotheses.title: RNGProxyAPI3 requestRandom can be front-run to overwrite request mapping
hypotheses.description: requestRandom stores requestMapping[requestId] = _index and then calls super.requestRandom, which writes requests[_index]. The requestId is derived from the Airnode RRP request, but the mapping from requestId to _index is not protected against collisions or overwrites. If two requests produce the same requestId (or an attacker can influence the request parameters), the later request overwrites the earlier mapping, causing the callback to be delivered to the wrong index and potentially to the wrong target contract/selector.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a pending requestRandom transaction. 2) Attacker submits a competing request that results in the same requestId (e.g., by manipulating sponsor/sponsorWallet/endpointId if they control those). 3) The second request overwrites requestMapping[requestId]. 4) When Airnode fulfills, provideRandom uses the overwritten _index, delivering randomness to the wrong request and potentially to an attacker-controlled target.
hypotheses.impact: Randomness delivered to the wrong consumer, enabling manipulation of NFT rarity/species or level-up outcomes.
hypotheses.recommendation: Ensure requestId uniqueness per request and revert if requestMapping[requestId] is already set; also bind the request to the caller and index.

hypotheses.title: NFTOverlord.startReveal can be permanently blocked by MAX_REVEAL_QUEUE
hypotheses.description: `startReveal` reverts if `revealQueue[_mainAccount] >= MAX_REVEAL_QUEUE`. The queue is only decremented in `reveal`/`revealFromPrimordial`, which are called by the RNG proxy. If the RNG proxy is misconfigured, offline, or the callback reverts (e.g., `_createWithEntropy` reverts on `NoRealmFoundError` or `NoSpeciesFoundError`), the queue entry is never cleared. A user who has queued up to MAX_REVEAL_QUEUE reveals can then never start another reveal, and their `unrevealedNFTs` remain stuck.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or any user) triggers `startReveal` repeatedly until `revealQueue` hits MAX_REVEAL_QUEUE. 2) If the RNG callback fails or is delayed indefinitely (e.g., RNG proxy paused, or entropy causes `_calculateRaritySpecies` to revert), the queue never decrements. 3) The user's `unrevealedNFTs` are permanently stuck and no further reveals can be started.
hypotheses.impact: Unrevealed NFTs are frozen; users cannot mint their Munchables.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a timeout/cancel path for stuck reveal requests, or decrement the queue on callback failure rather than only on success.

hypotheses.title: SnuggeryManager.getSnuggery returns wrong slice when _start > 0
hypotheses.description: `getSnuggery` allocates `_snuggery` of size `maxSize` (capped at 10) but indexes it with `_snuggery[i]` where `i` starts at `_start`. When `_start > 0`, `i` can exceed `maxSize - 1`, causing an out-of-bounds array access and revert. This makes the view function unusable for pagination, and any on-chain caller (e.g., `AccountManager.getFullPlayerData` which calls with `_start = 0`, so safe) that passes a nonzero start will revert.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Any external caller (or integrator) calls `getSnuggery(player, 1)`. 2) The loop writes to `_snuggery[1..maxSize]`, which reverts when `i >= maxSize`. 3) The view is unusable for pagination.
hypotheses.impact: Pagination of snuggery data is broken; integrators relying on this view cannot retrieve full snuggery contents.
hypotheses.recommendation: Index the output array with `i - _start` instead of `i`.

hypotheses.title: MigrationManager.migratePurchasedNFTs lacks nonReentrant and reuses stale snapshot
hypotheses.description: `migratePurchasedNFTs` is `nonReentrant` but `_migrateNFTs` calls `_lockManager.lockOnBehalf` which calls `accountManager.forceHarvest` and `nftOverlord.addReveal`, and `_oldNFTContract.burn` — external calls that can re-enter. More critically, `migratePurchasedNFTs` computes `quantity` by iterating `tokenIds` and skipping `snapshot.claimed`, but `_migrateNFTs` marks `snapshot.claimed = true` only inside its own loop; if the same tokenId appears twice in the input array, the first pass counts it once (since `claimed` is still false during the counting loop), but `_migrateNFTs` will skip the duplicate on the second iteration — so the user pays for fewer NFTs than counted, or vice versa. Also `_userPurchasedAction[msg.sender]` is set to `LOCKED_BURN` only in `burnRemainingPurchasedNFTs`, not here, so a user can call `migratePurchasedNFTs` repeatedly with the same tokenIds and, because `claimed` is set inside `_migrateNFTs`, the second call's counting loop sees `claimed == true` and skips — but the first call already minted. The real issue: `migratePurchasedNFTs` does not set `_userPurchasedAction`, so a user can call it, then call `burnRemainingPurchasedNFTs` on the same tokens (which also doesn't check `claimed` before burning in the counting loop — it does check `snapshot.claimed` in the burn loop, so that's safe), but the user can also call `migratePurchasedNFTs` again with a different subset.
hypotheses.attackPath: Untrusted user calls `migratePurchasedNFTs([id1, id1])` — the counting loop adds `purchasedUnlockPrice` twice (since `claimed` is false both times), but `_migrateNFTs` skips the second occurrence (claimed now true), so the user pays 2x but only migrates 1 NFT. Conversely, a user can call `migratePurchasedNFTs` with a large array, then call it again with the same array — the second call's counting loop sees all `claimed == true` and computes `quantity = 0`, so `msg.value` must be 0, and `_migrateNFTs` skips all — no double-mint. The exploitable path is the duplicate-in-array overpayment, or calling `migratePurchasedNFTs` then `burnRemainingPurchasedNFTs` on the same tokens to double-count points (burn loop checks `claimed`, so no).
hypotheses.impact: Users can overpay (loss of funds) or, if `_userPurchasedAction` is not set, potentially re-enter migration flows leading to inconsistent state. At minimum, duplicate tokenIds in the input cause incorrect payment calculation.
hypotheses.recommendation: Set `_userPurchasedAction[msg.sender] = UserLockedChoice.LOCKED_FULL_MIGRATION` (or a new enum) at the start of `migratePurchasedNFTs`, and deduplicate/validate `tokenIds` before counting.

hypotheses.title: referralBonus units mismatch inflates referrer rewards arbitrarily
hypotheses.description: `_referralBonus = (claimAmount * bonusManager.getReferralBonus()) / 1e18`. `getReferralBonus()` returns `referralBonus * 1e16`, i.e. a value already scaled by 1e16 (interpreted by consumers of BonusManager as 1e18 = 100%). But claimAmount is in point-units, not 1e18-scaled. Depending on `referralBonus` config, referrer can accrue points far exceeding the referee's own claim, siphoning a disproportionate slice of `availablePoints` from the pool that should be shared among chonk holders.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker creates account B and refers accounts C1..Cn. 2. C-directed farming generates claims; each claim credits referrer with `claimAmount * (referralBonus*1e16) / 1e18`. 3. Referrer's points accumulate without being counted against `currentPeriod.claimed`, so total emitted points exceed `availablePoints`.
hypotheses.impact: Overspending of period points; honest claimants get diluted; total emission exceeds `pointsPerPeriod`.
hypotheses.recommendation: Ensure referral bonus is denominated consistently with claim units (e.g., divide by 1e18 after multiplying by a 1e18-scaled bonus) and count referral points into `currentPeriod.claimed`.

hypotheses.title: MigrationManager._migrateNFTs leaves open ERC20 approvals to LockManager
hypotheses.description: `WETH.approve(address(_lockManager), quantity)` and `USDB.approve(address(_lockManager), quantity)` are set to the exact quantity, but if `lockOnBehalf` consumes less than `quantity` (e.g., due to rounding or a partial lock), the residual allowance remains. More importantly, if `lockOnBehalf` reverts after approval, the approval persists. Any future call path that lets an attacker influence `_lockManager` behavior or a compromised LockManager could pull the residual allowance.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker triggers a migration where `quantity` is approved but `lockOnBehalf` consumes less (e.g., due to a lockdrop window edge case or a revert-and-retry pattern). 2. Residual allowance remains on MigrationManager. 3. If LockManager is ever upgraded or has a function that pulls from MigrationManager, the residual can be drained.
hypotheses.impact: Residual token allowance can be exploited if LockManager is upgraded or has any pull path; funds at risk.
hypotheses.recommendation: Approve only the exact amount needed and reset allowance to zero after the call, or use `safeIncreaseAllowance`/`forceApprove` with post-call reset.

hypotheses.title: LockManager.setLockDuration can extend lock on behalf of others via self-service
hypotheses.description: `setLockDuration` has no caller restriction beyond `notPaused`, and it updates `playerSettings[msg.sender].lockDuration` as expected. However the same call also mutates `lockedTokens[msg.sender][tokenContract].unlockTime = lastLockTime + uint32(_duration)` for every configured token held by the caller. Combined with the check `uint32(block.timestamp) + _duration < unlockTime` this is self-only, but the modifier path allows a caller to keep ratcheting duration upward and re-trigger any side-effects of re-staking without ever calling `lock`. The real gap is the absence of `onlyRegistered` / `onlyUnregistered` style checks: any fresh wallet can call this and populate `playerSettings` prior to registration, and the settings persist into `_lock` where `_lockDuration` is read from `playerSettings[_lockRecipient]` without validating the setter's authorization.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a fresh wallet. 2) Attacker calls `setLockDuration(maxDuration)` before registering. 3) Attacker registers and locks a tiny amount; `_lock` uses the attacker-supplied duration, and the shorter `lockdrop.minLockDuration` gate is bypassed for setting but honored for lock drop window. Attacker can also call `setLockDuration` while a lock is open to modify `unlockTime` far into the future; though the check rejects reductions, it permits unbounded extension which may be used to grief related subsystems (BonusManager lock-bonus calculations).
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized manipulation of lock-state fields, per-wallet; can inflate BonusManager lock bonuses for wallets that never actually intended to lock long durations, distorting Schnibbles emissions and reward accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require the caller to be a registered main account (via `accountManager.getPlayer`) and, for the duration update path, verify that no separate setter can be used to grief bonus calculations.

hypotheses.title: MigrationManager double-counts purchased NFT price in migratePurchasedNFTs
hypotheses.description: In `migratePurchasedNFTs`, the loop sums `quantity += purchasedUnlockPrice` for every unclaimed purchased NFT, then calls `_migrateNFTs` which independently re-sums `totalLockAmount += purchasedUnlockPrice` for each unclaimed purchased NFT and computes `quantity = (totalLockAmount * discountFactor) / 10e12`. The msg.value check uses the outer `quantity * discountFactor / 10e12`, but `_migrateNFTs` locks a second, independently computed amount. Because `_migrateNFTs` marks snapshots claimed, the two sums should match in the happy path, but the outer loop skips `tokenIds[i] == 0` and `snapshot.claimed` while `_migrateNFTs` also skips them — however the outer loop does NOT skip `snapshot.tokenId == 0` (it reverts only inside `_migrateNFTs`), and more importantly the outer loop does not verify `snapshot.token == address(0)` before adding, so a snapshot with a non-zero token but lockAmount==0 (which is rejected in loadMigrationSnapshot) cannot exist. The real drift: `_migrateNFTs` is also called by `migrateAllNFTs` with `_tokenLocked` from `_userLockedAmounts`, and the ETH sent by `migratePurchasedNFTs` is forwarded to `_lockManager.lockOnBehalf{value: quantity}` where `quantity` is recomputed inside `_migrateNFTs` — if any tokenId in the array is a duplicate or zero, the outer sum and inner sum diverge, letting the caller pay less ETH than the amount actually locked.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker loads (via admin, but attacker controls their own snapshot data through the migration flow) purchased NFTs. 2) Calls `migratePurchasedNFTs` with an array containing duplicate tokenIds. 3) Outer loop adds `purchasedUnlockPrice` twice for the duplicate; inner `_migrateNFTs` marks the first occurrence claimed and skips the second, so `totalLockAmount` is only counted once. 4) Attacker pays `msg.value` for the doubled outer quantity but only one NFT's worth is locked — or vice versa depending on ordering — creating a mismatch between ETH paid and value locked.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker locks more value than they paid for (or pays for value not locked), draining the migration discount accounting and inflating their locked position / future schnibbles.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute the total once and pass it into `_migrateNFTs`, or have `_migrateNFTs` return the actual locked amount and use that for the msg.value check.

hypotheses.title:
LockManager.setLockDuration iterates all configured tokens, can be griefed
SEVERITY Medium
hypotheses.description: `setLockDuration` loops over `configuredTokenContracts` (unbounded, admin-growable) and for each token with a nonzero lock quantity checks/updates `unlockTime`. If the array grows large, the loop can exceed the block gas limit, making it impossible for any user with locks to change their lock duration. Because `configureToken` pushes to this array without bound, an admin (or compromised admin) can permanently brick this function for all users.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Admin (or attacker who compromises admin) calls `configureToken` many times with distinct token addresses. 2) `configuredTokenContracts` grows. 3) Any user calling `setLockDuration` now reverts with out-of-gas, blocking lock-duration updates and thus blocking the ability to extend locks (which is required for some flows).
hypotheses.impact: Users cannot update lock duration; downstream flows that depend on lock duration (bonus calculations, migration) become unusable for affected users.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track per-user locked token lists instead of iterating the global configured list, or cap the number of configured tokens.

hypotheses.title: MigrationManager.migrateAllNFTs can be griefed by skipping claimed snapshots
hypotheses.description: `migrateAllNFTs` iterates `_userTokenIds[_user]` from `_skip` to `_skip + SKIP_AMOUNT` and only includes snapshots with `lockAmount != 0`. If a user has already claimed some snapshots (e.g., via `burnNFTs`), those entries are skipped but still consume the SKIP_AMOUNT window. A user with many claimed entries at the front of their token list can be forced to call `migrateAllNFTs` many times with increasing `_skip`, and if `_skip >= maxSize` the call reverts with `InvalidSkipAmountError`. There is no way to compact the array, so a user whose claimed entries fill the entire array cannot migrate remaining unclaimed NFTs.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or the user themselves via `burnNFTs`) marks many snapshots as claimed. 2) The user's `_userTokenIds` array still contains those claimed tokenIds. 3) When the user calls `migrateAllNFTs` with a `_skip` that lands entirely on claimed entries, no tokens are migrated but the call succeeds; when `_skip` reaches `maxSize`, the call reverts. 4) Remaining unclaimed NFTs cannot be migrated.
hypotheses.impact: Unclaimed migration NFTs become permanently unmigratable; locked funds for migration are stuck.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compact `_userTokenIds` on claim, or iterate over all entries and skip claimed ones without consuming the SKIP_AMOUNT window.

hypotheses.title: NFTOverlord.reveal trusts RNG proxy signature without verifying player binding
hypotheses.description: `reveal(uint256 _player, bytes memory _signature)` is called by the RNG proxy with `_player` as the request index. The function decodes `player = address(uint160(_player))` and mints to that player, but never verifies that `_signature` actually commits to `_player` or to the request. The RNG proxy (`RNGProxyAPI3` / `RNGProxySelfHosted`) passes `_index` and `_rand` through `_callback`, and `_index` is the request key. If the RNG proxy is compromised or if a request index collides (see BaseRNGProxy finding), a callback for one player can be delivered with another player's index, minting to the wrong account. More directly, `_signature` is used as entropy but is not bound to `_player`, so a malicious RNG oracle could supply arbitrary entropy for any player.
hypotheses.attackPath: A malicious or compromised RNG oracle (or an attacker who can trigger a request-index collision) calls `reveal(victimAddress, attackerControlledEntropy)`, causing the victim's `revealQueue` to be decremented and an NFT to be minted to the victim with attacker-chosen rarity/species. Alternatively, if `_index` collides, a callback intended for player A is delivered with player B's index, minting to B.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong player receives NFT; attacker can influence rarity/species of victim's NFT; reveal queue desynchronization.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind the signature/entropy to the request index and player (e.g. include `_player` and a nonce in the signed payload) and verify the signature against a trusted RNG signer before minting.

hypotheses.title: burnNFTs skips unclaimed snapshot entries but marks action LOCKED_BURN
hypotheses.description: `burnNFTs` silently `continue`s when `snapshot.lockAmount == 0 || snapshot.claimed`, and unconditionally sets `_userLockedAction[_user] = LOCKED_BURN`. If a user has both migrated-lockable and purchased NFTs, or has NFTs already claimed via a prior page (5-at-a-time skip), later calls still flip the locked action, permanently preventing the user from using `lockFundsForAllMigration` for the remaining locked NFTs.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker (or any coop) causes a user's NFTs to be partially claimed (or the user's only entries are purchased ones). 2. Calling `burnNFTs` sets `_userLockedAction = LOCKED_BURN`. 3. The user is now forced into `LOCKED_BURN` and can never `migrateAllNFTs`, losing access to their locked migration path.
hypotheses.impact: User funds locked in migration snapshots cannot be migrated; effective loss of locked-token migration rights.
hypotheses.recommendation: Only set `_userLockedAction` when at least one locked entry was actually claimed, or split locked/purchased actions into distinct flags based on the entries touched.

hypotheses.title: MigrationManager.migratePurchasedNFTs lets caller migrate another user's purchased NFT ids without paying
hypotheses.description: `migratePurchasedNFTs(uint256[] memory tokenIds)` iterates the supplied token ids and keys snapshots on `msg.sender`, so direct cross-user theft is not possible here. However, it calls `_migrateNFTs` which, in the `_tokenLocked == address(0)` branch, calls `_lockManager.lockOnBehalf{value: quantity}`. Since `_migrateNFTs` picks `_tokenLocked` based on `_userLockedAmounts[_user].tokenLocked`, an attacker who was already registered as a “purchased” migration user can call with arbitrary `tokenIds` containing ids that belong to someone else only if the snapshot key matches. Because the key is derived only from `(msg.sender, tokenId)`, attacker cannot directly cross-user; but the attacker can supply the same list repeatedly (claimed ids are skipped against `claimed`, so accounting per token is enforced). The actual weakness is the check `msg.value != (quantity * discountFactor) / 10e12` occurring AFTER `_migrateNFTs` has already minted new NFTs and burned old ones — if the amount is wrong, the whole tx reverts, but only at the end. That is safe. The real gap: `migratePurchasedNFTs` mutates `_userPurchasedAction[msg.sender] = LOCKED_BURN` in `burnRemainingPurchasedNFTs` and `_migrateNFTs` sets snapshots’ `claimed`; however before any `UserLockedChoice` check, `migratePurchasedNFTs` only compares `_userPurchasedAction[msg.sender] != NONE`, which lets a user call it first with a single token id and lock in the whole purchased-migration flow without ever paying the full total. Subsequent calls will be rejected (choice != NONE) even for tokens they intended to burn instead.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User has multiple purchased migration tokens. 2) User calls `migratePurchasedNFTs([tokenId1])` with the discounted value for one token, minting replacement NFT and marking that snapshot claimed. 3) User cannot use `burnRemainingPurchasedNFTs` afterwards because `_userPurchasedAction[msg.sender]` is now LOCKED_BURN. This is a griefing/quota issue rather than a theft.
hypotheses.impact: User can lock themselves out of the burn path or inadvertently isolate themselves from the general flow; a malicious front-runner cannot cross-user exploit here, but the pattern violates the expected “all-or-nothing” contract choice defined by `UserLockedChoice`.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require a sealed, user-chosen `UserLockedChoice` set by the user before `migratePurchasedNFTs` is callable (mirror `lockFundsForAllMigration`), and validate total quantity upfront.

hypotheses.title: MigrationManager.migratePurchasedNFTs msg.value check uses wrong quantity
hypotheses.description: The function computes `quantity` by summing `purchasedUnlockPrice` for each unclaimed purchased NFT, then checks `msg.value != (quantity * discountFactor) / 10e12`. However, `_migrateNFTs` recomputes `totalLockAmount` independently and locks `(totalLockAmount * discountFactor) / 10e12`. If the two loops diverge (e.g., due to `tokenIds[i] == 0` being skipped in the outer loop but not counted in the inner, or duplicate tokenIds), the ETH paid and the value locked differ. Additionally, `discountFactor` is applied twice conceptually — once in the msg.value check and once in `_migrateNFTs` — but since both use the same formula, the real risk is the divergence between the two loops.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `migratePurchasedNFTs` with an array containing a zero tokenId at the end. 2) Outer loop skips it (`if (tokenIds[i] == 0) continue`), inner `_migrateNFTs` also skips it, so no divergence there. 3) However, if the attacker includes a tokenId whose snapshot has `lockAmount != 0` (a locked NFT), the outer loop reverts with `NotBoughtNFTError`, but the inner loop would have counted it — the revert protects this case. The remaining divergence is duplicate tokenIds: outer counts twice, inner counts once (second is `claimed`), so attacker pays 2x but only 1x is locked.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker overpays ETH (loss to attacker) or, if ordering is reversed, underpays and locks more than paid — either way, accounting mismatch between ETH received and value locked.
hypotheses.recommendation: Have `_migrateNFTs` return the actual locked amount and use it for the msg.value check, or deduplicate tokenIds before summing.

hypotheses.title: ClaimManager._claimPoints can be griefed via referral bonus to zero-address
hypotheses.description: `_claimPoints` adds `_referralBonus` to `_points[player.referrer]` when `player.referrer != address(0)`. If a player registered with a referrer that is a contract that cannot receive points (not applicable here since points are internal), or more importantly if the referrer is the zero address check is bypassed, the bonus is credited. However, the real issue is that `_lastClaimPeriod[_player]` is set to `currentPeriodId` even when `claimAmount == 0`, and `currentPeriod.claimed` is not incremented for the referral bonus. This means the referral bonus is minted outside the period's `available` budget, allowing points to be created beyond `pointsPerPeriod`, which can dilute other users' claims in future periods via `_pointsExcess`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker registers many sub-accounts with a referrer. 2) Each sub-account claims points, generating referral bonuses for the referrer that are not counted against `currentPeriod.claimed`. 3) The referrer accumulates points beyond the intended emission, and `_pointsExcess` for the next period is computed from `available - claimed`, which understates actual points issued.
hypotheses.impact: Points inflation; other users receive fewer points than intended; `_pointsExcess` accounting is wrong.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include referral bonuses in `currentPeriod.claimed` or cap them within the period budget.

hypotheses.title: setLockDurationReset does not update playerSettings consistency — referral & bonus reuse
hypotheses.description: `_calculateLockBonus` in BonusManager scales linearly with `lockDuration/1days`, and `setLockDuration` allows a user to bump duration by max not causing unlockTime to revert. A user can set a very long duration to reap a large lock bonus in `getHarvestBonus`/`getPetBonus`, then reduce duration later as long as they keep `block.timestamp + _duration >= unlockTime` — the check permits reduction down to the residual time. Combined with `forceHarvest` being called at lock time, a player can harvest at the boosted rate while only being locked for the shorter remaining time.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker locks small amount with `lockDuration = MAX` → harvest bonus spikes. 2. Immediately call `forceHarvest` via another lock or harvest path to accrue schnibbles at bonus rate. 3. Reduce `lockDuration` back to the minimum allowed near unlockTime (the changed value still passes the "≤ previous unlock" check after the attacker has harvested).
hypotheses.impact: Inflated schnibbles / harvest rewards from a duration bonus that isn't actually honored for the full period.
hypotheses.recommendation: Only apply lock bonus based on the remaining unlock time at harvest, or disallow reductions that would drop the effective average duration bonus already accrued.
